Ultralytics 8.4.174 also includes tracktrack (CVPR 2025), fasttrack and deepocsort configs; I could not verify their benchmark numbers.
code: boxmot 12.0.x (installed): HybridSort, DeepOcSort, BotSort, StrongSort, BoostTrack, plus boxmot.gsi interpolation. Ultralytics 8.4 trackers as a second implementation. No training.

technique: Adapt ReID to each match: self-supervised from tracklets, or few-label closed-set player classification (about 3-6 short labelled tracklets per player)
what_it_does: With only about 10-12 identities per game, a small per-match model (fine-tuned ReID, or a classifier on tracklet embeddings) learns cues specific to these players (shoes, socks, hair, build). Positives come from within unambiguous tracklets; negatives come from tracklets visible in the same frame.
evidence: Maglo et al., CVPRW 2022 (rugby sevens, offline, about 6 annotated tracklets per player). IDF1 on three games: 76.8, 84.3, 82.2, versus ByteTrack's 48.8, 54.9, 60.3 (about +26 points on average). ID switches 17/21/7 vs 26/23/14. With about 3.5 annotations per player, IDF1 is still about 75%. SUSHI with fine-tuned ReID: SoccerNet AssA 75.55 to 79.36. CLIP-ReIdent: fine-tuning lifts CLIP ViT-L/14 player ReID from 66.8 to 96.9 mAP. CAMELTrack's per-dataset BPBReID scores 81.8 mAP on SportsMOT but only 34.4 on DanceTrack (uniform clothing), which shows how hard same-kit identity is without adaptation.
applicability: Step 1 (no labels): from boxmot tracklets, keep the confident, isolated ones as pseudo-identities. Fine-tune OSNet x1_0 (about 2.2M params) for a few epochs with triplet or InfoNCE loss; this takes minutes on the RTX 2070 SUPER. Use same-frame tracklets of the same team as hard negatives. Step 2 (optional labels): a small UI to tag 3-6 short clips per player. The same labels give you the ground truth for IDF1/HOTA with TrackEval, which you currently lack, so every other change here becomes measurable. Then classify tracklets into player IDs instead of clustering.
code: No turnkey repo for Maglo's method (rugby dataset released). Use torchreid or boxmot OSNet backbones plus a small PyTorch training loop; sklearn/TrackEval for evaluation.

technique: Embedding quality gating plus temporal aggregation: confidence-gated EMA online; tracklet galleries with mean and minimum/percentile pairwise distance offline; best-view camera selection
what_it_does: Stops occluded, truncated, blurred or tiny crops from contaminating identity features, and summarises each tracklet robustly rather than by its latest frame.
evidence: StrongSORT ablation (MOT17-val): replacing the feature bank with an EMA update (alpha=0.9) gave +0.4 IDF1 and +1.2 FPS. Deep OC-SORT dynamic appearance: alpha_t = alpha_f + (1-alpha_f)(1-(s_det-sigma)/(1-sigma)), with alpha_f=0.95, so low-confidence (occluded) detections barely update the track. On DanceTrack-val this adds +0.33 HOTA on top of a fixed EMA. CAMELTrack, SportsMOT-val: EMA appearance alone reaches 76.0 HOTA versus 79.2 with a learned temporal encoder, so better temporal aggregation is worth about 3 HOTA. McByte++ keeps one averaged descriptor per finished tracklet for re-entry (cosine threshold 0.8, mutual best match). The Constructor.Tech GSR pipeline uses both the tracklet mean and the minimum pairwise distance. GTA averages over all box pairs.
applicability: Embed a crop only when: it overlaps no other box (IoU < 0.1, and no other foot point within about 1 m on the pitch); the box is at least about 60 px tall; it is not at a frame edge (distortion or truncation); and it comes from whichever camera shows the player larger or less occluded. The two diagonal cameras make this choice possible. Weight crops by detector confidence. Per tracklet, keep the mean plus 5-10 medoid embeddings. Linking cost = min(mean distance, 20th-percentile pairwise distance). Online inside boxmot, DeepOcSort already applies the confidence-gated EMA.
code: Built into boxmot DeepOcSort (alpha_fixed_emb) and StrongSort (ema_alpha). The offline part is a few dozen lines of numpy.

technique: Deep-EIoU: expansion IoU with an iterative scale-up schedule plus ReID, no Kalman filter (the sports-specific online association recipe)
what_it_does: Enlarges both boxes by a scale E before computing IoU, so fast, direction-changing players still overlap their next detection. Association is iterative: confident matches are taken at a small expansion, then the expansion grows for the rest. It drops the linear-motion Kalman assumption.
evidence: SportsMOT test: 77.2 HOTA / 79.8 IDF1 / 67.7 AssA, versus OC-SORT 73.7, MixSort-OC 74.1, BoT-SORT 68.7, ByteTrack 64.1. SoccerNet with oracle detections: 85.44 HOTA vs OC-SORT 78.09 and BoT-SORT 77.00. As a drop-in, EIoU lifts ByteTrack from 62.8 to 67.5 and BoT-SORT from 68.7 to 71.3 HOTA. Parameters: E starts at 0.7 and rises 0.1 per iteration over 2 iterations (high-score stage); 0.7 for low-score; 0.5 for unmatched; tau_A 0.25; tau_EIoU 0.5; 60-frame buffer. About 14.6 FPS on an RTX 4080 for the full pipeline. Used by the SoccerNet GSR 2025 winner (KIST) and the SoccerTrack 2025 winner, where it went from ByteTrack's 0.42 HOTA and 630 IDSW to 0.54 HOTA and 325.5 IDSW.
applicability: Not in boxmot 12. It is about 50 lines on top of boxmot BotSort's matching (expand both boxes, loop over scales) or the original repo with your detections. It suits small far-side boxes in cam2, where relative displacement per frame is large, and sudden cuts where a Kalman filter overshoots. The pitch-plane analogue is a distance gate that grows with time since last seen, which you can also add to the fused tracker.
code: github.com/hsiangwei0903/Deep-EIoU (Python 3.7 / torch 1.13 environment, no license stated). Includes a demo for custom video; the ReID weights are the sports OSNet from the ReID finding above.

technique: Part-based and lower-body descriptors: separate stripe or part embeddings, with the bib or torso region masked or down-weighted
what_it_does: The bib covers the torso, so a global embedding mostly encodes team. Part-based features (head/hair, shorts, legs/socks/shoes) keep the cues that differ between teammates and hold up better under partial occlusion.
evidence: PRTreID (MMSports 2023), SoccerNet-Tracking with ground-truth detections: part-based tracklet linking reaches 90.84 HOTA / 82.03 AssA, versus 85.7 / 77.25 with global features. On SoccerNet ReID, part-based BPBReID scores 71.43 mAP versus 62.63 (BoT) and 63.61 (PCB); PRTreID scores 72.59. With YOLOv8 detections, PRT-Track scores 59.77 HOTA / 74.44 IDF1 vs StrongSORT 54.86 / 65.1. The CLIP-ReIdent authors note that with identical kits, shirt number, shoes and face become the important cues. Gap: no published ablation isolates lower-body or shoe features for sports ReID, so validate on your own data.
applicability: Compute 2-3 horizontal-stripe embeddings with the same OSNet (upper body/head, shorts, lower legs and shoes), or use YOLO-pose keypoints to crop the bib out. Within a team, weight the lower stripes more. At 30-80 px tall, shoes are only a few pixels, so use these features only from the nearer camera. Adopt them only if the same-team verification AUC (from the ReID finding above) improves.
code: BPBReID / PRTreID: github.com/VlSomers/Prtreid (Hippocratic licence; weights and training via SoccerNet sn-gamestate/TrackLab, not standalone). KPR from the same group for occlusion. Stripe pooling on boxmot OSNet needs no training.

technique: McByte / McByte++: training-free ByteTrack-style tracking that uses propagated segmentation masks only when IoU matching is ambiguous
what_it_does: Propagates a mask per track (Cutie in McByte; EdgeTAM in McByte++). When several track-detection pairs are ambiguous by IoU, it subtracts the mask-box overlap from the cost. That separates crossing players whose boxes overlap. McByte++ adds an OSNet ReID check when a new tracklet starts, for re-entries.
evidence: DanceTrack test: McByte 67.1 HOTA / 68.1 IDF1, vs Hybrid-SORT 65.7, Deep OC-SORT 61.3, ByteTrack 47.7. SoccerNet: 85.0 vs OC-SORT 82.0. Ablation on DanceTrack-val: 47.1 to 62.3 HOTA when the mask is gated to ambiguous cases; using the mask everywhere hurts IDF1. Roboflow re-run with default parameters: DanceTrack 67.2 vs BoT-SORT 57.8; SportsMOT 76.5 vs 73.8. Speed: McByte 1.0-3.6 FPS. McByte++ (arXiv Aug 2026) runs 8.7-19 FPS; SportsMOT 79.9 HOTA online and 81.5 with GTA; SoccerNet 87.5 and 88.6 with GTA.
applicability: Per camera only (image space), and well suited to fixed tripods with frequent crossings. At 30 fps a 3-minute clip is about 5,400 frames per camera, roughly 25-90 min at 1-3.6 FPS, which is acceptable offline. On the 8 GB RTX 2070 SUPER, lower Cutie's max_internal_size. Check that the SAM/Cutie dependencies install on Python 3.14; otherwise use a separate env. Feed it your YOLO detections (--det_path) and still follow with GTA-style linking.

technique: CAMELTrack: learned multi-cue association (transformer over appearance, box and keypoint cues), for later once some labelled footage exists
what_it_does: Replaces hand-tuned cost fusion (IoU + EMA appearance) with a small trained association model on top of off-the-shelf detection and ReID. It learns when to trust appearance and when to trust motion, which matters during occlusions and among look-alikes.
evidence: DanceTrack test: 66.1 HOTA (69.3 with keypoints) vs Deep OC-SORT 61.3 and Hybrid-SORT 65.7. SportsMOT test: 80.4 HOTA / 84.8 IDF1 vs Deep-EIoU 77.2 / 79.8. Oracle study: perfect association with the same cues would add 15.5 HOTA on DanceTrack and 8.3 on SportsMOT, so the headroom is in association, not detection. Training takes about 1 hour on one consumer GPU. Full pipeline about 13 FPS on MOT17. It uses BPBReID with a SOLIDER Swin backbone (81.8 mAP on SportsMOT) and RTMPose.
applicability: This matches your diagnosis that recall is not the bottleneck. It needs labelled tracks to train (the labels from the per-match adaptation finding), or try the SportsMOT checkpoint zero-shot per camera. It is an online tracker, so you would still run the GTA-style offline linking and constraint stages after it. Lower priority until simpler fixes are measured.
